topics.title: Fischer, Champaran and a persistent peasant

learn.hook: A poor, unlettered farmer follows Gandhi from city to city until he agrees to come. That stubbornness changed Indian history.
points: Author: Louis Fischer, an American journalist. 'Indigo' is an extract from his book 'The Life of Mahatma Gandhi'.
Fischer heard the story from Gandhi himself when he visited Gandhi's ashram at Sevagram in 1942.
Subject: Gandhi's Champaran movement of 1917 in Bihar for the indigo sharecroppers.
Rajkumar Shukla, a poor sharecropper from Champaran, met Gandhi at the annual Congress session at Lucknow in December 1916 and begged him to come.
Shukla was resolute: he followed Gandhi to Cawnpore and to his ashram near Ahmedabad until Gandhi named a date and asked him to meet him in Calcutta.

example.q: What quality of Rajkumar Shukla made the Champaran movement possible?
steps: Gandhi was busy and kept putting him off.
Shukla followed him from Lucknow to Cawnpore to Ahmedabad.
His persistence finally won Gandhi's promise.
example.answer: His persistence and determination; he did not give up until Gandhi agreed to come.

learn.reallife: Ordinary citizens still move change in India through persistence: from RTI petitions to repeated letters that finally get a village road built.

topics.title: The road to Champaran and the tinkathia system

learn.hook: Three parts in twenty: that tiny fraction of land kept thousands of families in misery for years.
points: From Calcutta they went to Patna. At Rajendra Prasad's house (he was away), the servants took Gandhi for another poor peasant and would not let him draw water from the well, fearing he was an untouchable.
At Muzaffarpur, Professor J.B. Kripalani received him at the station at midnight with students; lawyers came to meet him too.
Tinkathia system: Champaran's sharecroppers were bound by contract to grow indigo on 15 per cent (3 parts in 20) of their land and give the whole crop to the British landlords as rent.
When Germany developed synthetic indigo, the indigo crop lost its value. Landlords then got the peasants to sign agreements to pay compensation for being released from the 15 per cent arrangement.

Gandhi met the secretary of the British landlords' association, who refused information to an 'outsider', and the British commissioner of the Tirhut division, who bullied him and told him to leave Tirhut.

example.q: Why was the landlords' demand for compensation unfair?
steps: Synthetic indigo had made the crop worthless to the landlords anyway.
They still made the peasants pay to be released from growing it.
So they profited twice from the peasants' ignorance.
example.answer: Indigo was no longer valuable, yet landlords made peasants pay compensation to end an obligation that had lost its worth.

learn.reallife: Exploitative contracts with poor farmers are not just history. India's debates on contract farming still ask how to protect sharecroppers from unfair terms.

learn.hook: An order says 'Leave'. A man writes back, politely, 'I will not.' Thousands of peasants arrive to watch what happens next.
points: Gandhi went to Motihari, the capital of Champaran. On his way to see a maltreated peasant, he was stopped and served an official notice to quit Champaran immediately.
He signed the receipt and wrote on it that he would disobey the order. He was summoned to court the next day.
In court he pleaded guilty, saying he had disobeyed not out of disrespect for the law but in obedience to the 'higher law of our being, the voice of conscience'.
Thousands of peasants gathered spontaneously at the court; the officials felt powerless. Gandhi helped them control the crowd.
Some days later the case was dropped on the orders of the Lieutenant-Governor. Civil disobedience had triumphed for the first time in modern India.

example.q: What does 'the higher law of our being, the voice of conscience' mean?
steps: Ordinary law is made by rulers.
Conscience is a person's inner sense of right and wrong.
When the two clash, Gandhi obeys conscience and accepts the penalty.
example.answer: Gandhi placed his moral sense of right above an unjust official order, and was willing to bear the punishment.

learn.reallife: Peaceful protest is part of India's democratic heritage. Civil disobedience means breaking an unjust law openly and accepting the penalty, not violence.

learn.hook: Why would a leader accept only half of what he asked? Because the real prize was not money.
points: An official commission of inquiry was set up; Gandhi was the sole representative of the peasants. Evidence went against the planters, and they agreed in principle to refund money to the peasants.
Gandhi asked for 50 per cent. The planters' spokesman offered 25 per cent, and Gandhi accepted, breaking the deadlock.
His reason: the amount was less important than the fact that the landlords had been forced to surrender part of the money and, with it, part of their prestige.
The peasants learnt that they had rights and defenders. Within a few years the British planters abandoned their estates, which went back to the peasants; indigo sharecropping disappeared.

example.q: Why did Gandhi accept a 25 per cent refund?
steps: He had asked for 50; the planters offered 25.
What mattered was that the landlords had to give back money at all.
That broke their prestige and showed peasants they had rights.
example.answer: Because the act of refunding broke the landlords' prestige and gave peasants courage; the amount was secondary.

learn.reallife: In negotiations, from wage talks to cricket board disputes, winning the principle often matters more than the exact amount. Gandhi knew this in 1917.

topics.title: Beyond politics: schools, health and self-reliance

learn.hook: Most leaders would leave after winning. Gandhi stayed on to open schools and teach villagers to keep clean.
points: Gandhi saw the deeper problems of cultural and social backwardness and opened primary schools in six villages.
Teachers included his disciples Mahadev Desai and Narhari Parikh with their wives, his youngest son Devdas, and his wife Kasturba.
Kasturba taught personal cleanliness and community sanitation. A doctor volunteered for six months with three medicines: castor oil, quinine and sulphur ointment.
Gandhi refused the help of C.F. Andrews, an English follower, because relying on an Englishman would show weakness; Indians had to rely on themselves.
Self-reliance and courage: the Champaran movement taught Indians to stand on their own feet.

example.q: Why did Gandhi refuse to let C.F. Andrews stay in Champaran?
steps: The lawyers wanted an Englishman on their side in an unequal fight.
Gandhi said this showed the weakness of their hearts.
The cause was just, so they had to rely on themselves.
example.answer: Depending on an Englishman would show weakness; Gandhi wanted Indians to be self-reliant.

learn.reallife: Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, launched in 2014 on Gandhi's birth anniversary, echoes what Kasturba taught in Champaran: sanitation is part of freedom.

topics.title: Themes: non-violence, rights and freedom from fear

learn.hook: 'The British could not order me about in my own country.' Gandhi called this a very ordinary thing. It was revolutionary.
points: Civil disobedience and non-violence: Gandhi broke an unjust order openly and peacefully, and accepted the penalty.
Peasants' rights: for the first time the peasants saw that they could stand up to the planters and win.
Freedom from fear: Gandhi told the lawyers that relief lay in freeing the peasants from fear, not in law courts.
Civil disobedience today: peaceful, lawful protest is part of democracy; it differs from violence or vandalism, and it means accepting legal consequences.

learn.hook: 'Why is Champaran called a turning point in Gandhi's life?' This question appears again and again. Here is how to nail it.
points: Shukla's persistence: he followed Gandhi from Lucknow to Cawnpore to Ahmedabad.
The 25 per cent refund: the principle and the surrender of prestige mattered more than the amount.
Impact on peasants: courage, rights, the end of indigo sharecropping; schools and sanitation in villages.
Turning point: Gandhi said it was the moment he decided the British could not order him about in his own country; it began freedom from fear for ordinary Indians.

Short answer on tinkathia: 15 per cent (3/20) of land under indigo, given as rent; compensation demanded after German synthetic indigo. Long answer on self-reliance: the Andrews episode, schools, sanitation.

example.q: Write a 50-word answer: Why did Gandhi consider Champaran a turning point?
steps: Point: he defied British authority openly for the first time in India.
Detail: refused to leave, pleaded guilty, case dropped.
Significance: showed Indians could win by non-violence, free of fear.
example.answer: At Champaran Gandhi first declared that the British could not order him about in his own country. His successful civil disobedience freed peasants from fear and proved that non-violent resistance could win, shaping the whole freedom struggle.
